name: Rosa Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I like that it's confidential, because I'd say things differently to my co-op's board than to my friends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small care co-op in a market town, which means the carers own a share of it, though as a new one my share is tiny. Most of my clients have dementia, so a visit is half personal care and half keeping someone calm and in the right day. My first call is Mr Brandt at eight, and if I rush him he won't let me near his shirt buttons, so I've learned to talk about his old allotment first. I drive the co-op's little electric car between villages, about six calls a morning and five in the evening. What wears me out is the evenings, and the forms, because I left school early and the medication charts still scare me a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what's already happening. Lots of talk, not much change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it to the other carers at handover: good, now can we talk about funding instead. Online I'd share posts about care being underpaid, which it is whether AI works or not. I'm not someone who posts much, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays exactly as tight as it is. The landlord put the rent up in September, and Tomas, my boyfriend, is a cook at the hotel on the square, so neither of us earns much. Our co-op lost a council contract in the spring, and nobody's said it out loud, but hours have been a bit thinner since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and I'd sign up for the nursing assistant course at the college in January, which I've been putting off for a year. I'd keep about four months of rent in the savings account. Maybe I'd use the AI on my phone to help with the course essays, since I already use it now and then to write emails to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Safe, but stuck. Like being told the bus is late but definitely coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned thinner hours. How many hours have you lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four a week since summer. That's real money for us, it's the difference between our weekly shop and the weekly shop plus a night out. If it got to eight, I'd have to pick up shifts with one of the big agencies, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you hate the big agencies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they do fifteen-minute calls. You can't do dementia care in fifteen minutes, you just can't. You walk in, she doesn't know who you are, and by the time she does, you're meant to be gone.

say: If AI flops, can we finally talk about **care funding** instead?
Care is **underpaid** whether AI works or not, and I'd share posts saying so.
think: My life stays **as tight** as now, with rent up and two low wages.
Our co-op lost a **council contract**, and my hours are already about four lower.
do: Enrol on the **nursing assistant course** at the college in January.
Keep about **four months of rent** in savings.
Use a phone **AI tool** now and then to help with course essays.
feel: **Safe but stuck**, like a late bus that's definitely still coming.
S0.quote: You can't do dementia care in fifteen minutes, you just can't.
fieldNote: Her pressure comes from **lost hours** after a contract loss, not from AI at all.
Strong pride in **slow dementia care**, and dread of fifteen-minute agency calls.
Already uses AI **now and then** for landlord emails, so the course essay idea is natural.

steps.text: Enrol on the college nursing assistant course in January
Keep four months of rent in the savings account
Use a phone AI tool to help draft course essays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office side changes and the hands-on side waits a bit. That fits what I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the co-op meeting that we should decide how we use it, not have it decided for us, because that's the whole point of a co-op. With friends I'd say I'm fine, my job is washing and lifting and talking, and a chatbot can't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paperwork part of my job goes first, and honestly, good. If AI does the medication charts and the care notes, I stop being scared of them. But I also think the big agencies get cheaper with AI rotas and beat us on price for contracts, and that's how we lose more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the AI care-notes tool once other carers say it works, not before. I'd push at the co-op meeting for us to buy it together so we don't fall behind the big agencies. And I'd still do the nursing assistant course, because it gives me something that isn't just this one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Hopeful about the forms, worried about the contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in your town, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The woman who does our scheduling, Hanne, she's been there twenty years and she does it all on a whiteboard and her phone. And Tomas's hotel would probably book everything with AI, but he's a cook, so he's fine. The receptionist there, not so much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try it first. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last new app we got lost three weeks of notes and I had to rewrite them from memory. I'm not going to be the first one again. When Dorota, who's been there ten years, says it works, I'll use it.

say: The co-op should **decide together** how we use AI, not have it decided for us.
A chatbot can't **wash, lift and talk** with my clients, so I'm fine.
think: The **paperwork** goes first, and I'd honestly be glad to stop fearing medication charts.
Big agencies with **AI rotas** could underbid us and cost us contracts and hours.
do: Use the **AI notes tool** only once trusted colleagues say it works.
Push the co-op to **buy tools together** so it keeps up with big agencies.
Carry on with the **nursing assistant** course.
feel: **Hopeful** about the forms and **worried** about the contracts.
S1.quote: If AI does the medication charts and the care notes, I stop being scared of them.
fieldNote: Welcomes AI for the **forms she fears**, which is a surprise from a cautious person.
The real threat she sees is **price competition** from big agencies, not robots yet.
Waits for **colleagues' proof** after an app once lost three weeks of notes.

steps.text: Try the AI care-notes tool once senior colleagues back it
Propose at the co-op meeting buying AI tools together
Keep going with the nursing assistant course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff and five for robots. That's quick. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say we need the government to protect care as human work, and to pay people while they retrain. I'd go to the protest if there was one. At work I'd say we need to stick together as a co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the co-op might not survive it. If a company can send a robot for less than our hourly rate by 2031, the council will buy that. The paperwork vanishing in 2028 helps me for three years, and then my hands aren't special either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd finish the nursing assistant course as fast as possible, because hospitals might keep humans longer than home care. I'd save harder, maybe from four months to six, by cooking at home every night with Tomas instead of our Saturday out. I'd join the care workers' union as well as the co-op, because the co-op alone is too small to be heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd have a list. A list helps me. It's when I don't have a list that I can't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hospitals might keep humans longer. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a hospital there are doctors watching, and families visiting, and somebody has to sign for things. In someone's home it's just you and them. Home care is where they'd try robots first, because nobody's watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not getting the bigger flat yet, and we're not getting a dog. He'd be upset about the dog. But I'd say let's give it till 2030 and see where we are.

say: Government should protect care as **human work** and pay people while they retrain.
I'd go to the **protest** and tell colleagues we need to stick together.
think: The **co-op might not survive** if robots cost less than our hourly rate by 2031.
Losing paperwork helps me for **three years**, and then my hands aren't special either.
do: Finish the **nursing assistant course** as fast as possible.
Raise savings from four to **six months** by cooking at home instead of Saturday nights out.
Join the **care workers' union** as well as the co-op.
feel: **Scared**, but steadier because she'd have a **list** of things to do.
S2.quote: Home care is where they'd try robots first, because nobody's watching.
fieldNote: She sees **home care** as more exposed than hospitals, where others watch and sign off.
Her plan is a **concrete list**, which she says is what keeps her calm.
Cancelling a **dog** and a **bigger flat** shows the household feeling it too.

steps.text: Fast-track the nursing assistant course at the college
Swap Saturday nights out for cooking at home
Join the care workers' union alongside the co-op
Put off the bigger flat and the dog until 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then robots around 2034. That gives me time to finish things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we shouldn't waste it, the government should fund training for carers right now. At the co-op I'd say let's plan how we stay useful, maybe by being the people who run the robots for clients who want a human around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right if I use the years. I'd be a qualified nursing assistant by 2028, maybe even working on a ward. The bit that worries me is that everybody in care will be trying to do the same thing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, then apply for a part-time bank shift at the district hospital to get ward experience. I'd use AI properly by then, because the other carers will have, and I'll follow them. I'd keep saving four months, not more, because I'd need some money for course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. It feels like a race I could actually finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone will try the same thing. What happens if the hospital doesn't take you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd stay at the co-op longer and try to be the one who knows the robots, I suppose. I'm not great with tech, but I'm good with an old man when he's frightened. Somebody will need to be there when the machine scares Mr Brandt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd spend on now that you wouldn't otherwise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The driving lessons for the bigger car licence, maybe, so I could do patient transport. It's about the cost of two months' food. Tomas thinks it's a good idea.

say: We have a **window**, and government should fund **carer training** now.
The co-op could be the people who **run the robots** for clients wanting a human.
think: If I use the years, I'm a **qualified nursing assistant** by 2028.
Everyone in care will try the **same escape** at the same time.
do: Finish the course and take **bank shifts** at the district hospital.
Learn the **AI tools** once other carers are using them.
Pay for a **bigger licence** to qualify for patient transport work.
feel: **Uneasy but manageable**, like a race she could actually finish.
S3.quote: I'm not great with tech, but I'm good with an old man when he's frightened.
fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **career plan**: nursing assistant, then hospital bank shifts.
She worries about a **crowded exit**, with all carers chasing the same jobs.
Sees her strength as **calming frightened clients**, not handling technology.

steps.text: Take part-time bank shifts at the district hospital
Use the AI tools once colleagues have them working
Pay for a larger vehicle licence for patient transport

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's when I'd be 40. It feels far but not that far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for not being ready with ten years, and I'd want the union to make the government promise a plan for carers. With friends, I'd say it's the one I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think by 2039 I'd want to be a nurse or something close, not a home carer. Ten years is enough to do the nursing assistant course and maybe even the full nursing degree part-time. I'd be the age my mum was when she went back to college, and she was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course next year, then save for two years toward the nursing degree. I'd learn whatever AI tools the co-op uses once they're proven. And I'd talk to Tomas about kids around 2030, because waiting forever for a safe moment doesn't work either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit uneasy, because the end is the same. But ten years is a lot of Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the end is the same. Does that change how you feel about this job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd enjoy it more, maybe, knowing it's not forever. I'd stop moaning about the evenings so much. I'd spend more time with the clients and less time worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope it turns into something like a service where a robot does the lifting and a human comes for company and checks. People would pay for that, I think. Whether the council would is another question.

say: With **ten years**, there's no excuse for not being ready.
The union should get the government to **promise a plan** for carers.
think: By 2039 I'd want to be **a nurse** or close to it, not a home carer.
Ten years covers the course and maybe a **part-time nursing degree**.
do: Take the nursing assistant course next year, then **save two years** for the degree.
Pick up the co-op's **AI tools** once they're proven.
Talk with her boyfriend about **having kids** around 2030.
feel: **Calmer**, though still uneasy because the end point is the same.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to do the nursing assistant course and maybe even the full nursing degree part-time.
fieldNote: A decade lets her picture a **nursing career** instead of a fight to keep this job.
Draws on her **mum's return** to college as proof that a late start works.
She'd stop waiting for a safe moment and plan **children around 2030**.

steps.text: Save for two years toward a part-time nursing degree
Start the nursing assistant course next year
Plan for a first child with her boyfriend around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the robots coming in 2031 for home care, where nobody's watching, and me still halfway through a course. What would help is the government paying carers to retrain while we still earn, and the co-op being big enough to have a say, maybe by joining with other co-ops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients' families. A lot of families feel guilty already that a stranger washes their mum. I think some would feel better with a robot, and some would feel much worse, and nobody's asked them.

headlineQuote: A lot of families feel guilty already that a stranger washes their mum.
portrait: A 27-year-old **dementia carer** at a small market-town care co-op, driving between villages.
Left school early, still **nervous of medication charts**, and planning a nursing assistant course.
Cautious with tech: uses AI **now and then**, and waits for trusted colleagues to prove tools.
Already **losing hours** after a lost contract, so AI Plateau still feels tight.
Moves from **scared** in AGI by 2028 to planning a **nursing career** in AGI by 2036.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots reaching home care by 2031 before she's finished retraining.
whatWouldHelp: Government **paid retraining** for carers while they still earn.
Co-ops **joining together** to have a say.
